clue.text: Violinist's stroke, melancholy weapon

blocks.note: feeling down is feeling melancholy
a bow is the archer's weapon

explanation.surface: A gloomy violinist treats the bow as a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The bow appears twice: the archer's weapon in the wordplay, the violinist's bow in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroke drawing the bow towards its tip, moving the hand away from the strings, is a basic bowing technique on string instruments.

clue.text: Free when put down after being picked up

indicators.note: in a vertical entry, lifting a word upward makes its letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to put someone down is to revile or disparage them

explanation.surface: Something is set free only once it has been lifted and then set down again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' and 'picked up' look like opposites of handling an object; one is an insult, the other turns that word upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver someone from evil or captivity is to rescue them, a biblical sense of setting at liberty.

clue.text: Run the show, as would American in pants?

blocks.note: first meaning: to be the one in charge, especially at home
second meaning, literal: Americans call trousers pants, so an American wearing pants is dressed in them

explanation.surface: Someone in charge is likened to an American dressed in pants.
explanation.walkthrough: To British readers pants are underpants, so the clue sounds faintly rude; in American English pants are simply trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes the dominant partner in a household who makes the decisions, historically said of a bossy wife.

clue.text: Cambridge rower perhaps went like the wind, did you say?

indicators.note: asking what was said points to how a word is heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: the wind blew; the past tense is pronounced the same as the colour

explanation.surface: A Cambridge oarsman sped along like the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is an Oxford or Cambridge student who has represented the university in a sport, such as the Boat Race; 'perhaps' marks the rower as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Students selected for university sport at Oxford or Cambridge earn a Blue, so a Boat Race oarsman is one instance.

clue.text: Monster fiction?

blocks.note: first meaning: something enormous
second meaning: a big lie, an outrageous untruth

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it looks like a genre of horror novel; the two words are separate meanings of one informal word.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the word means both an exceptionally large thing and a gross falsehood told with a straight face.

clue.text: Beef that brings home endless bacon?

definitions.text: Beef that brings home endless bacon?

blocks.clueFragment: Beef that brings home endless bacon?
blocks.note: surface reading: a joke about meat animals, beef somehow fetching pork

blocks.clueFragment: Beef that brings home endless bacon?
blocks.note: setter's reading: bringing home the bacon is earning money, so the beast is a business line that keeps earning

explanation.walkthrough: Beef suggests a bovine, and bringing home the bacon is the idiom for earning a living; endless earnings point to a reliable money-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Business jargon for a product or venture that generates steady profit with little further investment, like a cow milked repeatedly.

clue.text: Coin and ruby put in the middle

blocks.note: a cent is a small coin
ruby is a shade of red

explanation.surface: A coin and a ruby are set in the middle of something, perhaps a brooch.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruby reads as a gemstone beside the coin, but it is only supplying its colour.
explanation.definitionFit: To be placed at the midpoint is the past participle of the verb meaning to position at the core.

clue.text: Stuff in Seattle observed regularly

indicators.note: watching at regular intervals means looking at every other position only

blocks.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters of the city name

explanation.surface: Things are being watched routinely in Seattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' looks like a noun for possessions in Seattle; here it is a verb, to fill up.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff someone with food is to fill them completely, satisfying their appetite to the full.

clue.text: Raucous bird embraced by family, buzzard's ultimate fantasy

indicators.note: something embraced is held inside the arms of another, so one piece sits within another
ultimate means final, so only the closing letter of the word is used

blocks.note: a clan is an extended family
raucous means harshly loud
the cuckoo is a bird
last letter of the bird's name

explanation.surface: A buzzard dreams of a noisy bird kept by its family.
explanation.walkthrough: The family wraps the noisy bird after its first letter, and the buzzard's last letter closes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase, from Aristophanes' play The Birds, names an imaginary realm of absurdly unrealistic hopes, so it means a state of fantasy.

clue.text: Solver and setter back cowboy film

blocks.note: the solver and the setter together are us
the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: Solver and setter both endorse a cowboy movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like support, as in backing a film; it is the rear of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Films set on the American frontier featuring cowboys, outlaws and sheriffs form the genre named after that region.

clue.text: A felonious agent worked for former intergovernmental organisation

indicators.note: worked material has been shaped and reworked into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written, all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: A criminal spy was on the payroll of an old international body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked for' reads as employment; 'worked' is the signal and 'for' just links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Founded after the First World War and dissolved in 1946, it was the body that preceded the United Nations.

clue.text: Formal choice, very old tie, one must be thrown out

indicators.note: throwing something out removes it, and one stands for the single letter that looks like a numeral one

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
O is the abbreviation for old
taken as written

explanation.surface: A formal dress decision: a very old tie has to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is I, the Roman numeral, and that letter leaves the tie.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballot is an official expression of preference, a decision registered through a set procedure.

clue.text: A bit dissociated

blocks.note: taken as written
a bit is a portion or piece of something

explanation.surface: Someone is feeling somewhat detached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit' reads as 'slightly', modifying the last word; it is two pieces, the article and a portion.
explanation.definitionFit: Things kept separate or disconnected from one another stand at a distance, no longer joined.

clue.text: Doing little skid, lecturer's drunk

indicators.note: something drunk has been taken in, swallowed inside the words around it

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A tipsy lecturer is barely moving after a skid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' suggests an anagram, but nothing is rearranged; it means swallowed, with the answer sitting inside the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lazy or inactive is accomplishing hardly anything, an adjective for being unoccupied.

clue.text: Ousel flying in capital city

indicators.note: letters sent flying scatter and land in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written; an ousel is a blackbird

explanation.surface: A blackbird flies over a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: An ousel, also spelt ouzel, is an old name for the blackbird, making 'flying' natural in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the capital of South Korea, so it is one example of a national seat of government.

clue.text: Loudly demand massage

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so only the pronunciation of the next word counts

blocks.note: to demand something is to need it; the silent K leaves the sound unchanged

explanation.surface: Someone noisily insists on a massage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demand' and 'massage' sit as verb and object; each is a separate piece of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Masseurs work muscles by pressing and squeezing them with the hands, much as a baker works dough.

clue.text: King always beside dictionary – might one be ruminating?

definitions.note: a definition by example: the answer is one kind of ruminant

blocks.note: R for rex, Latin for king
OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A king who keeps a dictionary by him is surely a thoughtful sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruminating' looks like pondering; deer ruminate literally, chewing the cud. The king's letter is followed by the dictionary, then the poetic 'always'.
explanation.definitionFit: Deer are ruminants, animals that chew regurgitated cud, so this small European species is one such creature.

clue.text: Wear article in early summer month for Romeo

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit within it, so one piece lies inside another

blocks.note: to don clothing is to put it on and wear it
JUN is the calendar abbreviation for the first summer month
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Advice to a Romeo on what to wear in June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early' does double duty in the surface but here marks the abbreviated month; the article goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both names are bywords for a man devoted to wooing women, the legendary Spanish seducer and Shakespeare's lover.

clue.text: Hard filling trench from end to end

indicators.note: a filling sits inside whatever it fills

blocks.note: a trough is a long narrow channel
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Packing a whole ditch with hard material, from one end to the other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling' looks like a noun, as in hardcore filling a trench, but it is the verb that puts one piece inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Going right across or along something, entering at one side and leaving at the other, is the preposition's core sense.

clue.text: Athlete taking hour to enter tall building

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a tower is a tall building
HR is the abbreviation for hour

explanation.surface: An athlete takes an hour to get into a skyscraper.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the most general word in the clue; the field-event sense becomes clear only once the letters are built.
explanation.definitionFit: Discus, javelin, shot and hammer competitors are field athletes who hurl an implement for distance.

clue.text: Someone held label inside underwear

indicators.note: inside means within, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: hose are stockings or tights
a tag is a label

explanation.surface: Someone holds a garment's care label, sewn inside the underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Someone held' reads as someone gripping the label; it is the definition, a person held captive.
explanation.definitionFit: A captive detained to force demands on others is a person seized and kept against their will.

clue.text: A quid a kiss!

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for a pound sterling or a dollar; a quid is British slang for a pound
second meaning: a loud, smacking kiss

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like someone selling kisses for a pound each; the two halves are separate meanings of one slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang word names both a single banknote unit of currency and a noisy kiss planted on the lips.

clue.text: Fuddy-duddies, millions say?

definitions.note: a definition by example: a million is one such number

blocks.note: first meaning: old-fashioned, conventional people
second meaning: a million is a thousand times a thousand, so it is one example of a number multiplied by itself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Millions say' looks like a reported opinion of the masses; 'say' marks an example, and the arithmetic sense is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for staid, unfashionable people, and also the mathematical term for numbers formed by multiplying an integer by itself.

clue.text: Consider judge allowed to imprison leader of cartel

indicators.note: imprisoning locks something within walls, so one piece is held inside another
the leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: a ref, or referee, judges a game
let means allowed
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A judge weighs whether to permit locking up a drug cartel's boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a court official but is the sports referee in short form.
explanation.definitionFit: To think deeply or ponder something carefully is to turn it over in the mind, a synonym for considering.

clue.text: Defeat right away

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
someone away from home is out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right away' reads as 'immediately'; it splits into the abbreviation and a word for absent.
explanation.definitionFit: A rout is a crushing, overwhelming defeat, and as a verb it means to beat decisively.

clue.text: Matter in hanky initially wiped

indicators.note: wiping away at the start removes the opening letter

blocks.note: a tissue is a paper handkerchief

explanation.surface: Gunk in a handkerchief, wiped away first thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matter' plays on the surface as mucus in a hanky; as the definition it means a subject or concern.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter under discussion is a topic or question to be dealt with, the standard sense of a point at stake.

clue.text: Wood half stripped of bark

indicators.note: stripping away half leaves only the front portion of the word

blocks.note: taken as written before cutting
taken as written

explanation.surface: A log has half its bark peeled off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripped of bark' reads as a tree trunk peeled; 'of' is a piece of the answer, and the bark is a dog's.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's bark is rendered in English as this sound, so the word stands for the noise itself.

clue.text: Strike iron, say

definitions.note: a definition by example: an iron is one kind

blocks.note: first meaning: to hit with a heavy stick
second meaning: in golf, an iron is one type of stick used to hit the ball

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike iron' suggests a blacksmith at the anvil; the iron is a golfing implement.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for beating with a cudgel and a noun for the stick golfers swing, of which irons are a family.

clue.text: Piece of cotton wool, primarily sterilising wounds, afterwards binned

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each following word is taken

blocks.note: opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter

explanation.surface: A first-aid instruction: clean the wound with cotton wool, then throw it away.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words after the indicator supply their first letters, and the whole clue also describes how the answer is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pad of absorbent material used to clean wounds or take samples is exactly a dab of cotton wool.

clue.text: A children's game won hands down?

definitions.text: A children's game won hands down?

blocks.clueFragment: A children's game won hands down?
blocks.note: surface reading: a game won easily, without any effort

blocks.clueFragment: A children's game won hands down?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a race in which one child walks on their hands, palms down on the ground, while a partner holds their legs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Won hands down' is the idiom for an easy victory, but here it is literal: the competitors are running on their hands.
explanation.definitionFit: This sports-day event pairs children so one holds the other's ankles like barrow handles while the front child walks on their palms.

clue.text: Ridiculous bug traps brother or sister

indicators.note: a trap catches and holds something inside it

blocks.note: to bug someone is to annoy or rile them
sib is short for sibling

explanation.surface: An absurd insect catches a sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' reads as an insect doing the trapping; it is the verb meaning to irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: Laughable and absurd things provoke derision, which is what this formal adjective for ludicrous conveys.

clue.text: Correct fit around bottom

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to fit is to suit
a bed is the bottom of a river or sea

explanation.surface: Make sure clothing fits properly around one's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' suggests the body part; it is the floor of a river or sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspaper copy is checked and amended for errors by a sub-editor, so the verb means to revise text.
